title: Shellie Reid (LSNTAP) & Sam Harden (Pro Bono Net) — building AI guidance for legal aid and testing consumer models
pub: Talk Justice, An LSC Podcast, episode 72, host Cat Moon (Vanderbilt), YouTube / Legal Talk Network
author: Shellie Reid · Sam Harden

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts selective, risk-aware deployment and extends the cluster with concrete consumer-facing evidence: rapidly changing models call for adaptable guidance, while actionable next steps and disclaimers materially shape professionals’ assessments of usefulness and whether outputs constitute legal information or advice. It also applies this approach specifically to legal aid and access-to-justice tools.
qs: We’re trying to find a good group to gather, a group of organizations to develop guidance versus a policy, because with the speed that technology is changing in this AI area, policies would be outdated before we could even issue them.
People rated answers highly if they gave next steps, if they had an adequate disclaimer.

st.t: Justice augmentation: Activity exceeds proven access gains
st.an: The source aligns with the cluster’s framing of AI as a potential means to expand help for unmet civil legal need while stopping short of claiming demonstrated access or outcome gains. Its practical contribution is limited to recommending guidance resources and exploration, so it supports rather than materially extends the synthesis.
qs: I’m a lawyer and legal educator, and it’s part of my mission as a co-host of this podcast to engage in conversations with people who are thinking in new and different ways about how we can leverage technology to close the enormous civil justice gap we currently face in the US.

st.t: Justice capacity: AI potential requires deliberate implementation
st.an: The source aligns with the proposition that AI may help narrow the civil justice gap but requires purposeful guidance and practitioner engagement. Its recommended database and commentary are implementation resources, while the excerpts provide no testing results or evidence of improved access or legal outcomes.
qs: I’m a lawyer and legal educator, and it’s part of my mission as a co-host of this podcast to engage in conversations with people who are thinking in new and different ways about how we can leverage technology to close the enormous civil justice gap we currently face in the US.

st.t: Meaningful access: AI uptake cannot close justice gaps
st.an: The source aligns with the proposition that AI offers a conditional access-to-justice opportunity but that uptake alone is insufficient. It emphasizes practical guidance, risk awareness and informed decisions—including non-use—rather than claiming demonstrated justice-gap reductions.
qs: So it’s just trying to help people understand what things are capable of so that they can use the tools, because this is a great opportunity, I think, coming up for the world to help the access to justice and access to legal services space, if we can harness these tools for good.

So certainly, we try to provide resources that can help dispel those fears, that can educate and give the resources that attorneys need to make decisions and allow them to move forward with technology, if that’s their decision, or give them a basis for not using a technology.

st.t: Production model: Institutional absorption governs AI value
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s proposition that AI value and risk in access-to-justice settings depend on institutional preparation rather than tool availability alone. Reid urges legal-aid organisations to understand consumer AI and develop responsible recommendations because self-represented litigants will use it regardless of court readiness, while the decision to hold back formal policies reflects the cluster’s emphasis on cautious, readiness-dependent deployment.
qs: Shellie Reid: So I think practical guidance is we know that people, self-represented litigants, for example, are going to use technology whether the courts are ready for it or not.

So I think practical guidance for legal aid organizations to prepare and to know about this is to understand what can self-represented litigants who maybe have come to a legal aid organization and been turned down, or what can legal aid organizations recommend the use of these products.

kp.k: Crowdsourced guidance supports legal aid technology adoption
kp.d: Reid describes LSNTAP’s publicly available Airtable database of AI-related cases, attorney guidance, judicial opinions and bar materials. It grew from her own research need and community contributions; submissions are checked before publication. She reports approximately 60 items at the time of the conversation. The resource is intended to help attorneys understand developments and make informed technology decisions.
qs: So currently, we’re adding court cases, attorney guidance, judicial opinions, state bar ruminations, any guidance that we find that’s related to AI, current cases, anything that we can put that would be of use to attorneys in the field that need to know what’s going on.
we do go through and approve these items that are submitted so that we can verify the information before it goes up on our website.
this morning I was up in the 60 items listed in the database currently.

kp.k: Fear and restrictive messaging can inhibit experimentation
kp.d: Reid says attorneys’ fear of making mistakes extends to legal aid and nonprofit practice, and that some bar guidance reinforces those fears. She presents education as a way to support informed adoption or informed non-use rather than prescribing adoption universally. Moon separately advocates ethically recalibrating the profession’s relationship with risk.
qs: Many attorneys are afraid to try new things for fear of making mistakes.
we see state bar associations and even the national bar associations putting out guidance that also reinforces those fears in some respects.
allow them to move forward with technology, if that’s their decision, or give them a basis for not using a technology.

kp.k: Existing professional rules can address AI-related negligence
kp.d: Harden praises California’s proposal for building on MIT’s practical guidance and for stating that generative AI does not require new professional-responsibility rules. He treats the Avianca incident and other lawyers’ reliance on hallucinated material as technologically novel instances of negligence already covered by existing rules, not as evidence of a measured model error rate.
qs: they reiterated that even though this is a new technology, they didn’t think that it required issuing new rules of professional responsibility.

Other cases where lawyers have gotten burned for using ChatGPT hallucinations, that kind of thing is novel in terms of it being a novel technology. But that behavior, that negligence falls under the existing rules, as we already have them.

kp.k: Practice-of-law uncertainty threatens consistent consumer AI regulation
kp.d: Harden contrasts California’s invitation to reconsider the definition of legal practice with his reading of Florida’s chatbot-supervision recommendations. He worries that treating AI as potentially giving unlicensed legal advice could produce inconsistent state regulation, complicating vendor compliance and adoption. His examples of differing state approaches are hypothetical, not reported enacted rules. He prefers California’s practical approach without dismissing Florida’s guidance altogether.
qs: a lawyer has to supervise that ChatBot as if they’re, know, a paralegal or a legal assistant.

that kind of uneven regulatory structure would, frankly be a big problem for these technology companies and for widespread adoption of this technology because it’s hard to change behavior state to state in this kind of technology, and it’s hard to predict what states are going to do.
You can’t really predict with 100% accuracy what it’s going to say every time you use it, because it’s generative.

kp.k: Adaptable guidance should precede rapidly outdated policies
kp.d: Reid says LSNTAP is holding back on requested AI policies while seeking organizations to develop guidance instead, because technological change could outpace policy publication. She recommends understanding capabilities and limitations, including bias, hallucinations and risks from entering personally identifiable information. Her rationale includes preparing legal aid organizations for self-represented people who will use these tools regardless of institutional readiness.
qs: self-represented litigants, for example, are going to use technology whether the courts are ready for it or not.
with the speed that technology is changing in this AI area, policies would be outdated before we could even issue them.
they have the hallucination problem, they have problems putting personally identifiable information in them.

kp.k: Consumer AI may become public legal triage infrastructure
kp.d: Harden argues that people already turn to internet search for legal help and predicts that inexpensive consumer models and AI-integrated search will become legal triage systems for people without lawyers. He acknowledges limited visibility into behavior outside Pro Bono Net and legal aid systems, so the wider adoption trajectory is a prediction informed by observed search habits rather than a quantified finding.
qs: unless it’s a system that Pro Bono Net makes or that a legal aid organization runs, we’re not really seeing what people are doing.
Google is kind of like the default triage system for people that need legal help.
I really think that this new technology, considering how popular it has become and so quickly popular as well, people are going to be using it for solving legal problems.

kp.k: Experiments evaluated consumer models using real legal questions
kp.d: Harden describes feeding anonymized questions from a public Reddit legal-advice dataset into Bard, Claude, GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and Llama 2. He selected detailed questions that clearly signaled legal problems and recorded outputs in Airtable. An initial survey classified answers as legal advice or information; a second showed questions and full answers to legal professionals, asking about helpfulness on a one-to-five scale, actionable steps, hallucination, advice versus information and disclaimers. The transcript gives no sample sizes or numerical outcome distributions.
qs: My first experiment was taking a public data set, and it’s anonymized, it’s the questions that users of the Reddit legal advice, Reddit posted asking for legal help or legal information and feeding that into the popular chat models.
created an online survey where I asked legal professionals to go in and rate each response based on a number of factors.
people were able to say yes, no, or I don’t know if it hallucinated or not

kp.k: Disclaimers strongly shaped reviewers’ advice classifications
kp.d: Harden reports that most initial responses were classified as legal information, although a sizable percentage were classified as advice. Across the evaluation, models performed fairly similarly; GPT-3.5 was rated above GPT-4, which he cautions might reflect model timing and continuous updates. Reviewers favored actionable next steps and adequate disclaimers, with disclaimers strongly influencing advice-versus-information judgments. These are reported survey judgments, not legal determinations or proof of output accuracy.
qs: The majority of responses people rated as legal information, but there was a sizable percentage that people said was legal advice.
GPT-3.5, strangely, was rated higher than GPT-4.
Updates happen continuously, so this stuff is hard to fix at a point in time.
People rated answers highly if they gave next steps, if they had an adequate disclaimer.
If it didn’t have a disclaimer, no matter what the answer said, they said generally it was legal advice.

kp.k: Legal aid is exploring closed-system self-help chatbots
kp.d: Reid recommends harnessing AI to improve assistance and describes an experiment with an organization proposing a closed-system chatbot for legal aid self-help websites. She frames community benefit as something still to be tested, not demonstrated. She also urges organizations to understand what people find through search and use that knowledge to make self-help sites usable for their intended audiences.
qs: provide a closed system chat bot for legal aid self-help websites. So we’re experimenting with that.
Let’s see if what they can produce will provide the kind of benefit to the community at large.
use those things that are learned in creating the self-help website so that they’re usable for the people that they’re designed for.

kp.k: Consumer AI enables action beyond retrieving legal information
kp.d: Harden recounts a news story about a New York tenant who used ChatGPT to draft a landlord letter, then requested more legalistic wording. He reports that the landlord subsequently fixed problems and did not raise the rent. He treats this as an example of people taking affirmative steps with AI, while explicitly acknowledging that the landlord did not confirm the letter caused the outcome.
qs: she went back to ChatGBT and said, no, you need to insert more legalese into this letter, make it sound more like it’s from a lawyer.
the landlord fixed the problems and didn’t raise the rent
the landlord didn’t come out and say, well, I got this letter that sounded really legal and that made me decide to not do these things. But we can kind of assume that.
not just get legal information, but to actually take affirmative steps.

kp.k: Mainstream platforms may bypass dedicated legal aid websites
kp.d: Harden worries that users will remain within generative search rather than navigate to separate legal aid sites and chatbots. He invokes substantial page-to-page user attrition as a general user-experience argument, not a measured result from his legal AI experiments. Accordingly, he prioritizes guiding Microsoft, Google and other consumer platforms alongside developing specialized, ethically sourced legal chatbots.
qs: How many people are going to stay in search in that generative AI experience to help them versus using it to get to another website and then to talk to a separate chat bot.
creating like an ethically sourced chat bot with the right information is very important because people will be using that too.
the bigger target is to give guidance to companies like Microsoft and Google on what they should and should not be considering when people are asking their tools for legal help.

kp.k: Overbroad refusals can obstruct otherwise relevant legal help
kp.d: Harden reports that some tested models refused to answer questions mentioning past self-harm, even when the user was not asking how to harm themselves. He explicitly labels the presumed trigger as an assumption. He uses this observation to argue for community input into model governance about useful responses, actionable information and appropriate resources, beyond state-bar regulation of lawyers.
qs: some models, if the question included a mention about self-harm, like not someone asking how do I take affirmative steps to do this? But this happened in the past, the model would outright say, I can’t help you with that
I’m assuming here, but because of the mention of self-harm.
this is what’s helpful, this is what people need, this is the information that they can take action on, and these are the resources that your model should be returning.

kp.k: Professional responsibility extends to shaping public-facing AI
kp.d: Harden advocates coordinated outreach through organizations such as LSNTAP, LSC and the ABA to communicate public needs and AI’s benefits and harms to technology companies, while acknowledging uncertainty about how to organize engagement and the constraints of commercial secrecy. Moon separately frames helping people help themselves as an opportunity and obligation potentially greater than improving lawyers’ own productivity. Harden’s stated criterion is whether people obtain good help, rather than whether they hire lawyers.
qs: I don’t have a good answer to that.
not just how do we talk to lawyers about how to use this technology, but what is the message that we send to the technology companies on how is this affecting people in the real world?
in my book, if they’re able to use an AI tool to get good help, that’s a win.
that’s our greater opportunity and obligation, even above and beyond figuring out how it makes us more competent in delivering our own work.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Harden predicts that consumers will use widely available generative AI to solve legal problems, including taking action rather than merely seeking information.
pts.d: Harden links this expectation to rapid adoption, existing reliance on internet searches for legal help, and generative AI's incorporation into search. Reid similarly expects self-represented litigants to use technology regardless of court readiness. These are expectations and observations about direct public use, not claims that lawyer-supervised deployment is the only relevant model.

pts.k: Reid sees a conditional opportunity for AI to expand access to legal help; Harden argues that public-facing model guidance is especially important.
pts.d: Reid advocates legal aid experimentation, including a closed-system chatbot for self-help websites, without claiming demonstrated benefits from that project. Harden worries that users may remain within AI-enabled search rather than reach specialist legal aid websites. He therefore prioritises helping mainstream technology companies provide useful legal responses, alongside building specialist chatbots.

pts.k: Harden reports broadly similar model ratings, with GPT-3.5 rated above GPT-4, and a strong role for disclaimers and actionable steps in respondents' assessments.
pts.d: These are findings from Harden's exploratory surveys, not a general ranking of legal competence. He reports that respondents tended to rate answers more highly when they provided next steps and adequate disclaimers. Disclaimers also influenced whether respondents classified answers as legal information or legal advice; these classifications are respondent perceptions, not determinations of unauthorized practice.

pts.k: Harden warns that divergent state treatment of AI as practicing law could impede adoption, while existing professional rules already address lawyers' negligent reliance on fabricated output.
pts.d: Harden favours California's practical approach and its consideration of clarifying the practice of law. He interprets Florida's chatbot-supervision discussion as implying that an AI could give legal advice without a license. His examples of inconsistent state classifications are hypothetical, not a report of enacted differences. Separately, he argues that novel technology does not make the underlying negligence in hallucinated-citation cases a new category of professional misconduct.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Harden's model findings derive from two exploratory surveys using anonymized Reddit legal questions and five consumer models.
pts.d: Harden describes submitting public, anonymized Reddit legal-advice questions to Bard, Claude, GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and Llama 2. His first survey asked respondents to classify model answers as legal advice or information. His second presented questions and full answers to legal professionals, asking about helpfulness, actionable steps, hallucination, advice versus information, and disclaimers. The transcript supplies no sample sizes, numerical results, statistical tests or independently verified accuracy rates. Ratings of hallucination allowed an 'I don’t know' response.

pts.k: Claims about public use and access benefits rely on professional experience, an illustrative news report and ongoing experimentation rather than measured population outcomes.
pts.d: Harden explicitly acknowledges limited visibility into usage outside Pro Bono Net and legal aid systems. He recounts a news story in which a tenant used ChatGPT to draft a landlord letter, after which repairs occurred and rent was not increased; he acknowledges that the landlord did not confirm the letter caused those decisions. Reid's closed-system chatbot work remains experimental. Harden's regulatory analysis rests on his reading of California and Florida guidance and references to hallucinated-citation cases, including Avianca.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The discussion concerns current experimentation and an emerging transition, with no dated forecast; rapid model changes limit the durability of findings and policies.
pts.d: In the supplied 2023 source, public use is described as already occurring and likely to expand as AI enters search. Harden qualifies the GPT-3.5/GPT-4 comparison because model updates may affect results. Reid favours adaptable guidance over fixed policies because she expects the latter to become outdated too quickly. The regulatory warning is conditional on jurisdictions adopting inconsistent treatment.

pts.k: Access-to-justice gains depend on understanding limitations and configuring systems to provide useful help rather than inappropriate refusals or unreliable output.
pts.d: Reid identifies biased training material, hallucinations and personally identifiable information as risks that legal aid organisations must understand. Harden reports that some models refused legal questions mentioning past self-harm, while expressly qualifying his explanation of the cause as an assumption. Neither speaker offers a measured net benefit or claims that consumer AI is safe to rely on without qualification.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected group is people without lawyers, including self-represented litigants unable to obtain legal aid.
pts.d: The predicted change is greater direct access to legal information and assistance with concrete steps, alongside exposure to unreliable answers and unhelpful refusals. AI-enabled search may become the place where users remain for assistance, potentially reducing visits to specialist self-help resources. This is a civil justice gap discussion, not a claim about enterprise legal cost savings or law-firm job displacement.

pts.k: Legal aid organisations, lawyers, professional bodies and consumer AI companies face new education, design and coordination responsibilities.
pts.d: Reid describes attorney fear as an adoption barrier and positions practical resources as support for informed decisions about using or avoiding tools. Harden calls for the legal aid community and bodies such as LSNTAP, LSC and the ABA to coordinate guidance to technology companies about useful public-facing legal assistance. His concern about regulatory fragmentation particularly affects companies serving users across state borders.
